Sculptor King -- Lungelo Gumede [5399]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
It seems as if, at any moment, one of the 1.9m Nelson Mandela sculptured figures on display at the BAT Centre in Durban could come alive.
Artist Lungelo Gumede has masterfully worked in each line and curve on Tata’s face, and in so doing etched a sense of warmth in his smile and wisdom in the crinkle of his eyes.
The queue of Mandela wax sculptures from different stages of his life are among Gumede’s artworks at the BAT centre. His other works there include those of local and international celebrities and political figures.

Gumede, 30, of rural Ndwedwe, near Inanda, shot to international fame recently after a CNN interview.

It had art connoisseurs from around the world in search of him.

During the interview, Gumede was described as moulding Africa’s first wax museum from the ground up.
A trip to Madame Tussauds wax museum in New York forged a burning desire in him to showcase Africa’s waxwork masterpieces.

Gumede has always had an artistic hand. At school, he often drew pictures of his teachers.

“My mom wanted me to be a doctor, but she didn’t have enough money to send me to medical school, so I became an artist. I am living my dream and it gives me freedom to express myself.”

Gumede was awarded a bursary in 2004 to study fine art at the Durban University of Technology.

On Friday, he presented IFP president Mangosuthu Buthelezi with a life-size sculpture at the Durban ICC for his 90th birthday.

“Some of my statutes are my way of appreciating what the person has done for the world. At the time of sculpting Michael Jackson, I was playing his music.”

He said that his most challenging sculpture yet lived, for now, in his workshop behind his showroom.

It’s a life-size figure of Hugh Masekela with puffed cheeks, blowing into his trumpet, reminiscent of the days when he wowed audiences with his smooth and soulful jazz.

Lungelo has also just been awarded a R 20 million commission by the Ethekwini Municipality to create two 9m statues of Nelson Mandela and Oliver Tambo that will be erected outside the Durban City Hall.

However Durban has a fraught history of sculptures and memorials. Like many South African cities, it has a variety of colonial and apartheid statues. There are a variety of heroes Queen Victoria staue at the city hall. Dick King statue near the harbour, Jan Smuts, Louis Botha and Batholemew Diaz.

But there is a missing history and it is not reflected in the memorials that are dotted around the city.
For example there is no mention of the 16 year old boy, Ndongeni KaXoki, who accompanied Dick King and helped him on the journey.

In order to reflect the real history of our country several sculptures have been commissioned.
But there have been issues in their execution.

Statue of King Shaka Airport that was commissioned and then taken away from airport. Apparently the Royal Zulu household was dissapointed that King Shaka was depicted unarmed surrounded by cattle, instead of the great warrior that he was.

(They have now just completed a 7m statues of King Shaka as a warrior that will be placed at the airport later this year.)

https://www.news24.com/Travel/South-Africa/King-Shaka-statue-still-causing-trouble-20130823

In 2010 there were elephant sculptures that were made at the Warwick Triangle on the highway to the entrance of Durban. Work was stopped on the sculptures because the ANC felt that it was an endorsement of the IFP, as their logo has 3 elephants depicted in it. (An agreement was reached later that there would be a fourth elephant and the work was completed. The process took a while.)

https://mg.co.za/article/2013-02-01-andries-bothas-elephant-sculptures-to-be-completed-at-last

Then there was also the sculpture of King Dinuzulu that was not unveiled for over a year because his statue was not as high as Louis Botha' statue that is in same square.

https://www.iol.co.za/news/south-africa/king-dinuzulu-statue-to-be-unveiled-415218

Many argue that the statues reflect a colonial style of architecture. And to my knowledge the sculptures have been completed by white artists.


Other critics say do we need new statues when so much is wrong with Durban.
Should the money not be used elsewhere? But others argue that more sculptures should be made to reflect the history of South Africa and act as a commemorative focus for people.

Monuments are a means of asserting new group values, restoring dignity and self- esteem, expressing identity and recognising achievement. s with the recognition of African languages and other aspects of previously marginalised culture, monuments can be considered means of personal and community empowerment, which can contribute to the enhancement of self- esteem and thereby restore harmony in society. Post-apartheid monuments could thus be understood as a strategy of resolving conflict by fulfilling basic human needs that have been frustrated for a very long time.
This perspective might explain the urgency with which the project of constructing new monuments is currently being pursued in South Africa and the willingness to allocate substantial funds to such structures in a context of scarce resources.
Although the cost argument – frequently cited by those latently or openly opposed to new monuments – has its validity, it would be too simplistic sweepingly to disapprove of new monuments because we can’t afford them. As Thembinkosi Ngcobo, Executive Director of the eThekwini Department of Parks, Recreation and Culture, aptly put it (personal communication): ‘When highlighting the cost of erecting new monuments, one must also consider the cost of not doing the exercise. Monuments create a sense of belonging, which de facto many people currently don’t enjoy – especially in urban centres strutting with colonial and apartheid-era monuments.’
In order to resolve conflict and achieve reconciliation, it is significant that an official recognition, a public acknowledgement of pain and losses suffered in the past, take place (Ross 2000; Volkan 1997). Such acknowledgement can take the form of ritual actions, symbolic gestures and, particularly, monuments and memorials. All of these can facilitate, or help to complete, the process of mourning, which is essential in dealing with trauma and accepting loss. In conflict situations, coming to terms with the past is an important prerequisite for forgiveness or reconciliation.
Monuments and memorials not only facilitate mourning but also form a focal point for ritual actions (eg commemorative events on anniversary days), and a site for symbolic gestures (such as placing a wreath). By constituting a public, visible, lasting recognition they affirm the group identity that is based on such trauma, help to overcome loss, and pave the way for reconciliation. Contrary to those who advocate a moratorium on new monuments, it could be argued that we might need to build even more, although one might want to consider less costly options.
City Head Parks and Recreation Thembinkosi Ngcobo
Ndabo Langa – architect, jazz club owner, interested in aesthetics
Lungelo Gumede
Sihawu Ngubane – African Languages UKZN

Lungelo Script 6 Final

Red notes for Floris

V/O
Hidden in a basement in Durban, dozens of wax statues lie waiting to see the light of day.
This is the work of 33 year old Lungelo Gumede who wants to start South Africa’s first wax museum.

Lungelo
“I’ve got about plus 100 statues now that I have created. Ever since I went to Madame Tussauds, you can imagine I have been working towards fulfilling my dream to start wax museum.”

V/O
It’s something that has consumed him for the past 13 years.

Masa
“And here I really want to say, hello Mr President. Who do we have here?”

Lungelo
“Here we have our business moguls, as you can see we have billionaire Patrice Mostepe and then we have got Ubaba President uCyril Ramaphosa as a businessman.”

V/O
His collection also includes a few larger than life celebrities.

Masa
“Now Lungelo I see we have moved away from politics and here we have some movie stars.”

Lungelo
“Here we have movie stars, action heroes, Angelina Jolie, Morgan Freeman, terminator and 007, James Bond yes.”

Please add cow moo here

Link
Lungelo grew up in rural KZN. Although he could draw he did not know what art was, but his teachers recognisd his talent.

Lungelo
“Now and then the teacher would ask me to come and draw on the chalk board , they will give me a text book and I will draw whatever is in the textbook for the kids to learn , that is how I knew I was an artist.”

Masa
“So initially you didn’t know it was art?”




Lungelo
“I did not know it was art back then because we did not do art as a subject at school, so I only realised that after I finished matric.”

V/O
Nonhlanhla Gumede is Lungelo’s proud mother.

Nonhlanhla
“He started drawing at an early age. He was in Grade 1 or 2. Even though he was young he drew very realistically. He took a pen and paper and drew everything he saw.”

V/O

After school he continued to draw and was recognised by an artist at the BAT Centre, a community arts project in the Durban Harbour precinct, where he was introduced to formal art.
He was then was awarded a bursary to do fine art at the Durban University of Technology. When he was in second year, a work he painted of Mandela was auctioned for charity in New York and this trip opened Lungelo’s eyes to new opportunities. And one of the first places he visited in New York was Madame Tussauds.

Lungelo
“I didn’t know that they had this wax museum thing. I didn’t even know about the wax museum up until I went to Madame Tussauds. When I got there I see the statues and I had a background of sculpture and I looked at it and I felt like I want to do something like that, I was so excited. I had an interest in doing something like that. So when I came back to South Africa it was more like having a dream or working to a vision , one day I want to start something like that.”
V/O
Lungelo translated this passion and for the last 12 years he’s devoted himself to creating his own statues. He’s established a studio at the BAT centre and works every day on new faces. Unlike Madame Tussauds that measures their models with scientific accuracy, Lungelo bases most of his modelling using photographs. One of the people that Lungelo has sculpted in person, is Prince Mangosuthu Buthelezi, this sculpture was unveiled at his 90th Birthday party.
Buthelelezi

“I was very impressed that Lungelo Gumede at his age has been able to do what he is doing.It was done as a surprise gift by those, my children and those who arranged the birthday.That is all I can say about that.”

Please add wind noise here with Mandela statue – or country buzz

V/O
What role does public art play in South Africa?

Link
Public art not only helps us to collect our thoughts like Nelson Mandela”s capture site here in the Midlands but it also attracts people and creates conversation.

V/O
Lungelo’s just been comissioned to create two 9 m statues of Nelson Mandela and Oliver Tambo for the Ethekwini’s Municipality.

Masa
“What are you trying to communicate through your art.”

Lungelo
“Its more like educating people about the history of our country, about these icons and what these people did for us you know in our country, that’s the kind of message I am trying to send out there.”


V/O
This is Durban’s City Hall built in the early 1900’s at the height of Natal’s power, these monuments in front of the building reflect a selective and outdated history of a soverign Queen and Colonies.

Link
This Dick King statue much like South Africa’s colonial history does tell the full story, it’s missing a key figure, that is Undongeni KaXoki, Lungeni was a 16 year old who helped Dick King on his journey. While Dick King’s role in the story has been celebrated. Undongeni’s role has been reduced to a footnote in history.


Kim
“So the Dick King statue is a classic example of a hero being celebrated and another clear hero being omitted.”

V/O

Kim Goodwin runs the Goodwin Foundry in the Midlands. For the past 28 years he’s cast most of the major public art statues in Kwa-Zulu Natal.

Masa
“What are your views on public art?”

Kim
“The role of public art definitely in the past 25 years has been to highlight our struggle heroes, to try and re address so many problems that occurred in the past 200 years in this country and to some extent that has happened.

Up Sound “Wow this is impressive.”

Kim
“So while it is a celebration the story behind every piece of public art is a lot more complicated than the public realise.”


V/O
And Durbans had it’s fair share of complications. King Shaka’s statue at the airport was removed because the Royal family was allegedly not happy that he was depicted as a cow herd. Elephants sculptures commissioned for the 2010 Soccer World Cup were halted for 4 years because they looked too much like the 3 elephants in the IFP logo. It was only completed when an extra elephant was added.

Thembinkosi Ngcobo is head of Parks, Recreation & Culture at eThekwini Municipality.

Masa
“Do you think as a city Durban has a good balance in historical representation?”


Thembinkosi
“No city in South Africa currently can claim to have that. People have different experiences, so these experiences have to be captured and become part of the soul of the city, without them being represented they are not going to feel part of the social cohesion.”

V/O
Lungelo is showcasing his Madiba collection in his own gallery in Umhlanga .

Masa
“Lungelo this looks amazing , it’s looks real it really does, take us through this work. I see a young Madiba here.”

Lungelo
“Oh ja, this is when Madiba was 17 years old and we have this one when he was a boxer and then from there he became a lawyer.”

V/O
He has a special affinity for the father of our nation.

Nonhlanhla
Mandela was the first person in his pictures.
He was the first important person that Lungelo drew.

Masa
“It’s such a treat to be seated around so many Mandelas, why the focus on him?”

Lungelo
“I thought because we are celebrating 100 years of Madiba, let me do something different, using my talent and making 27 statues of him for the 27 years he spent in prison , so I had to do my research from when he was younger until his death.”


Up Sound ‘Sawubona”


V/O
Lungelo’s work certainly causes a reaction. Through his work the spirit of South African icons live on. Under the watchful eye of Queen Victoria, Lungelo took one of his Madiba sculptures to the City Hall of Durban for a morning.


Thembinkosi
“History is there for us to, no matter good or bad, to learn from it ,observe from it and then make decisions about the future. So our view is that these colonial statues that are there they are fine, but what would be wrong is for them not to be contextualised.”


V/O
Like Louis Botha, who stood alone in this park for decades, was contextualised when King Dinuzulu was added in 2008. Louis Botha released King Dinuzulu from prison as an act of reconcilliation and the statues are meant to represent a sign of peace between the two camps.

But there are already Mandela statues in Johannesburg, Pretoria and Cape Town, does Durban need another one?

Thembinkosi
“Durban is the only city in the world where Mandela voted for the first time, Durban is the only city of the world where he was elected as the president of the ANC. So this city has a very unique experience of Nelson Mandela and we need to capture that.”




Masa
“How do you feel about your young boy you saw drawing is now going to create this 9m statue of Nelson Mandela.”

Nonhlanhla
“I am very happy and I know he will manage because he is a hard worker.

V/O
It’s reported that the Ethekwini Municipality has set aside R 20 million for these statues. Which may sound like a lot of money, but the costs of casting two 9 m statues in bronze are high.
Their commission has drawn criticism, because Ethekwini Municipality has many competing priorities.

Kim
“I don’t buy that argument at all any kind of celebration that is out there for the public to enjoy to be challenged by intellectually I think is well ,well worth it.”

V/O
Lungelo’s on track to start his wax museum. He may be the first black sculptor in South Africa, to create such large works of our liberation heroes.

Masa
“How does that make you feel?”

Lungelo
“I feel good, I feel good. I feel very happy, laugh, very happy.”

Promo 1

Here we have the entertainment section

With over 100 statues completed Lungelo Gumede is set to start his own wax museum, like the famous Madame Tussauds in the heart of Durban.


Promo 2
Sawubona up sound

V/O
Mandela on the streets of Durban. 33 year old Lungelo Gumede’s vision is set to change the art landscape, he wants to create a wax museum and bring the South African heroes to the people.



Promo 3

Born in rural Kwa-Zulu Natal with little art training, 33 year old Lungelo Gumede has become the rock star of sculpting, and is set to start the first wax museum in South Africa.

So when I came back to South Africa it was more like having a dream or working to a vision , one day I want to start something like that.” V/O Lungelo translated this passion and for the last 12 years he’s devoted himself to creating his own statues. He’s established a studio at the BAT centre and works every day on new faces. Unlike Madame Tussauds that measures their models with scientific accuracy, Lungelo bases most of his modelling using photographs. One of the people that Lungelo has sculpted in person, is Prince Mangosuthu Buthelezi, this sculpture was unveiled at his 90th Birthday party. Buthelelezi “I was very impressed that Lungelo Gumede at his age has been able to do what he is doing.It was done as a surprise gift by those, my children and those who arranged the birthday.That is all I can say about that.” Please add wind noise here with Mandela statue – or country buzz V/O What role does public art play in South Africa? Link Public art not only helps us to collect our thoughts like Nelson Mandela”s capture site here in the Midlands but it also attracts people and creates conversation. V/O Lungelo’s just been comissioned to create two 9 m statues of Nelson Mandela and Oliver Tambo for the Ethekwini’s Municipality. Masa “What are you trying to communicate through your art.” Lungelo “Its more like educating people about the history of our country, about these icons and what these people did for us you know in our country, that’s the kind of message I am trying to send out there.” V/O This is Durban’s City Hall built in the early 1900’s at the height of Natal’s power, these monuments in front of the building reflect a selective and outdated history of a soverign Queen and Colonies. Link This Dick King statue much like South Africa’s colonial history does tell the full story, it’s missing a key figure, that is Undongeni KaXoki, Lungeni was a 16 year old who helped Dick King on his journey. While Dick King’s role in the story has been celebrated. Undongeni’s role has been reduced to a footnote in history. Kim “So the Dick King statue is a classic example of a hero being celebrated and another clear hero being omitted.” V/O Kim Goodwin runs the Goodwin Foundry in the Midlands. For the past 28 years he’s cast most of the major public art statues in Kwa-Zulu Natal. Masa “What are your views on public art?” Kim “The role of public art definitely in the past 25 years has been to highlight our struggle heroes, to try and re address so many problems that occurred in the past 200 years in this country and to some extent that has happened. Up Sound “Wow this is impressive.” Kim “So while it is a celebration the story behind every piece of public art is a lot more complicated than the public realise.” V/O And Durbans had it’s fair share of complications. King Shaka’s statue at the airport was removed because the Royal family was allegedly not happy that he was depicted as a cow herd. Elephants sculptures commissioned for the 2010 Soccer World Cup were halted for 4 years because they looked too much like the 3 elephants in the IFP logo. It was only completed when an extra elephant was added. Thembinkosi Ngcobo is head of Parks, Recreation & Culture at eThekwini Municipality. Masa “Do you think as a city Durban has a good balance in historical representation?” Thembinkosi “No city in South Africa currently can claim to have that. People have different experiences, so these experiences have to be captured and become part of the soul of the city, without them being represented they are not going to feel part of the social cohesion.” V/O Lungelo is showcasing his Madiba collection in his own gallery in Umhlanga . Masa “Lungelo this looks amazing , it’s looks real it really does, take us through this work. I see a young Madiba here.” Lungelo “Oh ja, this is when Madiba was 17 years old and we have this one when he was a boxer and then from there he became a lawyer.” V/O He has a special affinity for the father of our nation. Nonhlanhla Mandela was the first person in his pictures. He was the first important person that Lungelo drew. Masa “It’s such a treat to be seated around so many Mandelas, why the focus on him?” Lungelo “I thought because we are celebrating 100 years of Madiba, let me do something different, using my talent and making 27 statues of him for the 27 years he spent in prison , so I had to do my research from when he was younger until his death.” Up Sound ‘Sawubona” V/O Lungelo’s work certainly causes a reaction. Through his work the spirit of South African icons live on. Under the watchful eye of Queen Victoria, Lungelo took one of his Madiba sculptures to the City Hall of Durban for a morning. Thembinkosi “History is there for us to, no matter good or bad, to learn from it ,observe from it and then make decisions about the future. So our view is that these colonial statues that are there they are fine, but what would be wrong is for them not to be contextualised.” V/O Like Louis Botha, who stood alone in this park for decades, was contextualised when King Dinuzulu was added in 2008. Louis Botha released King Dinuzulu from prison as an act of reconcilliation and the statues are meant to represent a sign of peace between the two camps. But there are already Mandela statues in Johannesburg, Pretoria and Cape Town, does Durban need another one? Thembinkosi “Durban is the only city in the world where Mandela voted for the first time, Durban is the only city of the world where he was elected as the president of the ANC. So this city has a very unique experience of Nelson Mandela and we need to capture that.” Masa “How do you feel about your young boy you saw drawing is now going to create this 9m statue of Nelson Mandela.” Nonhlanhla “I am very happy and I know he will manage because he is a hard worker. V/O It’s reported that the Ethekwini Municipality has set aside R 20 million for these statues. Which may sound like a lot of money, but the costs of casting two 9 m statues in bronze are high. Their commission has drawn criticism, because Ethekwini Municipality has many competing priorities. Kim “I don’t buy that argument at all any kind of celebration that is out there for the public to enjoy to be challenged by intellectually I think is well ,well worth it.” V/O Lungelo’s on track to start his wax museum. He may be the first black sculptor in South Africa, to create such large works of our liberation heroes. Masa “How does that make you feel?” Lungelo “I feel good, I feel good. I feel very happy, laugh, very happy.” Promo 1 Here we have the entertainment section With over 100 statues completed Lungelo Gumede is set to start his own wax museum, like the famous Madame Tussauds in the heart of Durban. metadata.Further information: It seems as if, at any moment, one of the 1.9m Nelson Mandela sculptured figures on display at the BAT Centre in Durban could come alive. Artist Lungelo Gumede has masterfully worked in each line and curve on Tata’s face, and in so doing etched a sense of warmth in his smile and wisdom in the crinkle of his eyes. The queue of Mandela wax sculptures from different stages of his life are among Gumede’s artworks at the BAT centre. His other works there include those of local and international celebrities and political figures. Gumede, 30, of rural Ndwedwe, near Inanda, shot to international fame recently after a CNN interview. It had art connoisseurs from around the world in search of him. During the interview, Gumede was described as moulding Africa’s first wax museum from the ground up. A trip to Madame Tussauds wax museum in New York forged a burning desire in him to showcase Africa’s waxwork masterpieces. Gumede has always had an artistic hand. At school, he often drew pictures of his teachers. “My mom wanted me to be a doctor, but she didn’t have enough money to send me to medical school, so I became an artist. I am living my dream and it gives me freedom to express myself.” Gumede was awarded a bursary in 2004 to study fine art at the Durban University of Technology. On Friday, he presented IFP president Mangosuthu Buthelezi with a life-size sculpture at the Durban ICC for his 90th birthday. “Some of my statutes are my way of appreciating what the person has done for the world. At the time of sculpting Michael Jackson, I was playing his music.” He said that his most challenging sculpture yet lived, for now, in his workshop behind his showroom. It’s a life-size figure of Hugh Masekela with puffed cheeks, blowing into his trumpet, reminiscent of the days when he wowed audiences with his smooth and soulful jazz. Lungelo has also just been awarded a R 20 million commission by the Ethekwini Municipality to create two 9m statues of Nelson Mandela and Oliver Tambo that will be erected outside the Durban City Hall. However Durban has a fraught history of sculptures and memorials. Like many South African cities, it has a variety of colonial and apartheid statues. There are a variety of heroes Queen Victoria staue at the city hall. Dick King statue near the harbour, Jan Smuts, Louis Botha and Batholemew Diaz. But there is a missing history and it is not reflected in the memorials that are dotted around the city. For example there is no mention of the 16 year old boy, Ndongeni KaXoki, who accompanied Dick King and helped him on the journey. In order to reflect the real history of our country several sculptures have been commissioned. But there have been issues in their execution. Statue of King Shaka Airport that was commissioned and then taken away from airport. Apparently the Royal Zulu household was dissapointed that King Shaka was depicted unarmed surrounded by cattle, instead of the great warrior that he was. (They have now just completed a 7m statues of King Shaka as a warrior that will be placed at the airport later this year.) https://www.news24.com/Travel/South-Africa/King-Shaka-statue-still-causing-trouble-20130823 In 2010 there were elephant sculptures that were made at the Warwick Triangle on the highway to the entrance of Durban. Work was stopped on the sculptures because the ANC felt that it was an endorsement of the IFP, as their logo has 3 elephants depicted in it. (An agreement was reached later that there would be a fourth elephant and the work was completed. The process took a while.) https://mg.co.za/article/2013-02-01-andries-bothas-elephant-sculptures-to-be-completed-at-last Then there was also the sculpture of King Dinuzulu that was not unveiled for over a year because his statue was not as high as Louis Botha' statue that is in same square. https://www.iol.co.za/news/south-africa/king-dinuzulu-statue-to-be-unveiled-415218 Many argue that the statues reflect a colonial style of architecture. And to my knowledge the sculptures have been completed by white artists. Other critics say do we need new statues when so much is wrong with Durban. Should the money not be used elsewhere? But others argue that more sculptures should be made to reflect the history of South Africa and act as a commemorative focus for people. Monuments are a means of asserting new group values, restoring dignity and self- esteem, expressing identity and recognising achievement. s with the recognition of African languages and other aspects of previously marginalised culture, monuments can be considered means of personal and community empowerment, which can contribute to the enhancement of self- esteem and thereby restore harmony in society. Post-apartheid monuments could thus be understood as a strategy of resolving conflict by fulfilling basic human needs that have been frustrated for a very long time. This perspective might explain the urgency with which the project of constructing new monuments is currently being pursued in South Africa and the willingness to allocate substantial funds to such structures in a context of scarce resources. Although the cost argument – frequently cited by those latently or openly opposed to new monuments – has its validity, it would be too simplistic sweepingly to disapprove of new monuments because we can’t afford them. As Thembinkosi Ngcobo, Executive Director of the eThekwini Department of Parks, Recreation and Culture, aptly put it (personal communication): ‘When highlighting the cost of erecting new monuments, one must also consider the cost of not doing the exercise. Monuments create a sense of belonging, which de facto many people currently don’t enjoy – especially in urban centres strutting with colonial and apartheid-era monuments.’ In order to resolve conflict and achieve reconciliation, it is significant that an official recognition, a public acknowledgement of pain and losses suffered in the past, take place (Ross 2000; Volkan 1997). Such acknowledgement can take the form of ritual actions, symbolic gestures and, particularly, monuments and memorials. All of these can facilitate, or help to complete, the process of mourning, which is essential in dealing with trauma and accepting loss. In conflict situations, coming to terms with the past is an important prerequisite for forgiveness or reconciliation. Monuments and memorials not only facilitate mourning but also form a focal point for ritual actions (eg commemorative events on anniversary days), and a site for symbolic gestures (such as placing a wreath). By constituting a public, visible, lasting recognition they affirm the group identity that is based on such trauma, help to overcome loss, and pave the way for reconciliation. Contrary to those who advocate a moratorium on new monuments, it could be argued that we might need to build even more, although one might want to consider less costly options. City Head Parks and Recreation Thembinkosi Ngcobo Ndabo Langa – architect, jazz club owner, interested in aesthetics Lungelo Gumede Sihawu Ngubane – African Languages UKZN
